Le mois dernier, La Converse a publié un: Last month, La Converse published an article in response to the controversy surrounding Imane Khelif: <l1>“People need to get used to seeing strong women”</l1>. While I was researching that piece, a source close to La Converse pointed me to Sarah-Judith Hinse-Paré, also known by her stage name, Kayiri. I had never met a Black violinist, or even a competitive boxer who is also an artist, let alone someone who radiates so much joy!
Toutefois, au cours de notre rencontre,: Yet during our meeting, I heard a story that contrasted with that big smile. Kayiri excels at everything she undertakes, whether on stage or in the ring. But before rising to that level, the young woman faced everyday racism, harassment, depression and even domestic violence.
Pendant notre entretien, je craignais d’: During our interview, I was wary of bringing up these traumatic experiences, since I didn’t know where she was in her healing process. But she spoke about them with detachment: “Being a victim doesn’t mean being defeated,” she told me.
Je suis fière de vous présenter le portr: I’m proud to present the portrait of this inspiring woman!
Son deuxième prénom, Kayiri, d’origine b: Her middle name, Kayiri, which is of Burkinabè origin, evokes the ability to not let yourself be influenced and to dare to follow your own path. That is what she represents, and this one word – Kayiri – sums up the subject of this article perfectly.
Que l’on songe aux cordes d’un ring et à: Think of the ropes of a boxing ring and the strings of a violin, and it quickly becomes clear that few people manage to play both! Sarah-Judith Kayiri Hinse-Paré – a musician, author, composer, performer and Canada’s boxing vice-champion in her category – is a multifaceted force. La Converse met her in her recording studio in LaSalle to learn more about the unique world of this artist and athlete who refuses to be boxed in by the limits others have tried to impose on her.
« Kayiri est mon deuxième prénom, un pré: “Kayiri is my middle name, a Burkinabè name,” begins the young woman, whose style is resolutely hip-hop. “This name represents the ability to not be swayed by other people’s judgment and to dare to pursue your own aspirations. It suits me perfectly!” the artist and athlete exclaims, before adding: “I’ve often been asked to choose between sports and music, but for me, it was unthinkable to choose one at the expense of the other.”
Vêtue d’une veste en jean et d’une jupe: Dressed in a denim jacket and a matching skirt, Kayiri completes her look with a white and pink cap bearing her name. Her large earrings shaped like Africa sway gently, proudly celebrating her Burkinabè roots.
Originaire de Gatineau, Kayiri confie s’: Originally from Gatineau, Kayiri says she always felt marginalized because of her mixed-race skin colour. Her father is Black and her mother is white, and she grew up as a minority, something she felt keenly during her childhood. “Honestly, it was hard growing up in Gatineau. I felt like there weren’t many people who looked like me. In elementary school, I was the only Black kid, so I’m very lucky to have found music early on; it was my refuge… I wasn’t in my environment, I wasn’t free to be myself,” she concludes.
Dès l’âge de sept ans, Kayiri jongle ave: From the age of seven, Kayiri juggled sports and the violin, two passions that would never leave her. “I love creating, playing sports, moving,” she insists. “Even though I’ve explored different sports, the violin has been a constant in my life. As far back as I can remember, I’ve always done sports and music at the same time.”
C’est au cégep, après avoir vécu du harc: It was at CEGEP, after being harassed, that the young woman decided for the first time to set aside her athletic activities, which she would do for several years. “I’d rather not go into the details, but that period plunged me into depression,” she says tersely, not wanting to dwell on that episode of her life. “During that ordeal, I gained a lot of weight because I was eating my emotions,” she admits bluntly.
En 2010, elle déménage à Montréal pour é: In 2010, she moved to Montréal to study at the Conservatoire de musique de Montréal. Kayiri gradually regained her confidence as her music career took off. “An incredible world opened up to me,” she recalls enthusiastically. “I started playing with bands, performing more, and I even started travelling with my music.”
<strong>« Ç’a changé ma vie, de ressenti: “It changed my life to feel strong for the first time”
C’est aussi à ce moment-là que l’artiste: It was also around that time that the artist decided to take her health back into her own hands. When she walked into the Underdog gym, she never expected boxing to become an integral part of her life. “It’s funny, boxing was really not something I would have imagined doing,” she says with an amused smile. At first, she was simply looking for a gym to lose the weight she had gained during her years of depression.
Mais son coach, voyant son potentiel, lu: But her coach, seeing her potential, suggested something different. “He came up to me and said, ‘You’re really athletic. Maybe a combat sport would do you good.’ I told him, ‘No, I’m not violent,’” she recalls, bursting into laughter. “It’s true that I had a lot of prejudices about boxing. I thought it was evil. And yet… I’ve seen so many people transform,” she says with a faint smile. “I’ve seen guys who were in gangs go back to school, rebuild their lives. I transformed myself through boxing too.” In the same breath, she adds: “It changed my life to feel strong for the first time. To take back control of my abilities.”
Se remémorant ses débuts, elle poursuit: Looking back on her beginnings, she continues: “As a classical violinist, I was used to staying in the background, practising alone, without talking to anyone. But then, there was 20-year-old Kayiri, hitting pads with guys… It was incredible.”
« Finalement, je suis montée dans le rin: “Eventually, I got in the ring and started fighting. My first bout was pretty funny; I won very easily,” she says. “Then, right after the fight, I drove to Montréal because I was playing at a music gala.” She goes on: “Boxing demands an enormous amount of discipline, but so does music. To succeed, you have to set a schedule and clear goals, and stick to them. Right now, I’ve taken a break from boxing. I think there’s a balance to find, breaks to take. Now, I’m really going to push my music. I have a message to share,” she says.
<strong>Violence conjugale : « Qui aurai: Domestic violence: “Who would have thought it could happen to a boxer?”
Pour Kayiri, la musique est un exutoire,: For Kayiri, music is an outlet, a way to free herself from buried pain. Her latest single, Avoir le dessus, is one example. “I wrote this song during the pandemic, a period that allowed me to step back,” she says. “People asked me why I had slowed down my music releases, but the truth is that I was experiencing domestic violence,” she confides, her gaze piercing.
« Quand on pense à une boxeuse, on imagi: “When you think of a female boxer, you imagine strength, resilience. And yet, I was a victim of domestic violence. Who would have thought it could happen to a boxer? And yet, it happened.”
Après avoir partagé son histoire, elle a: After sharing her story, she realized how common it is. In combat sports, many women experience violence, but they often stay silent. According to the boxer, the reason for this silence is the shame these women feel. “The first feeling you have when you’ve been a victim of domestic violence is shame. When you become a victim, you feel ashamed, because you didn’t decide anything. It’s someone else who comes and commits an act, and it puts you in a category of victims,” she explains.
« Moi, c’est arrivé au même moment où on: “For me, it happened at the same time people were talking about femicides, during the pandemic. So I thought, ‘Oh! I’m one of those women,’” she says with a nervous laugh.
« Le lendemain où j’ai été étranglée par: “The day after my ex strangled me, I was so confused… I wondered how I could have been so naive, how I hadn’t seen it before. And then the shame kicks in. I’m a victim of domestic violence, the shame!” she exclaims. After a brief moment, she continues: “And some people don’t talk about it simply because they’re in denial. Many experience physical violence, but there’s also all the psychological and emotional violence that comes before the physical violence. For me, the physical violence only happened once – he strangled me – but the verbal abuse had started at the very beginning of the relationship.”
Si Kayiri peut aujourd’hui en parler, c’: Kayiri can talk about it today because she feels she is in a good healing process. “I’m very open to talking about it and being the voice of women who are in those situations. Being a victim doesn’t mean being defeated. You can overcome the worst ordeals and not let yourself be locked into the role of victim. You can decide to stop listening to those negative voices in your head,” she insists.
« Les histoires douloureuses font partie: “The painful stories are part of me, but they don’t define me: I have a choice between letting these ordeals slow me down or continuing to move forward, to achieve my dreams, to grow.”
Pour faire passer ce message de résilien: To spread this message of resilience and hope, Kayiri doesn’t limit herself to the stage. She is also involved with young people, notably through writing workshops she leads in schools. “Working with them lets me see how much contemporary culture, marked by violence in video games and negative influences, shapes their worldview and their energy,” she says. “I also do workshops in prisons with women,” she adds. Drawing on a journey marked by obstacles, Kayiri says she has a knack for forming deep connections with young people from all walks of life. “My experiences give me great empathy and an understanding of their reality.”
Kayiri encourage les jeunes à explorer l: Kayiri encourages young people to explore their dreams, to imagine horizons they may never have considered before, to open doors and to push past their limits. “For me, life is about constantly seeking to grow and become a better version of yourself,” she insists, her hands speaking as much as she does.
Son message est clair : « Vous pouvez ac: Her message is clear: “You can accomplish anything you want in life. Limits are a human invention. Great inventors and great creators often succeeded by going beyond what they were told was possible. If you come up against a limit, analyze it, adapt and keep moving forward. Don’t let yourself be held back by the limitations others impose. Follow your heart, pursue your dreams and don’t stop because of obstacles.”
